questions.questionText: An enterprise has fixed costs of $18,000, variable costs of $42,000 and output revenue of $75,000. Calculate gross margin and net farm income for this enterprise, assuming no other costs.
Explain cation exchange capacity (CEC), identify two factors that influence it, and discuss its importance in nutrient management.
questions.explanation: Clay minerals and humus carry negative charges that retain exchangeable cations such as Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺ and NH₄⁺.

questions.questionText: Describe the relationship between photosynthesis, respiration and net dry-matter accumulation in a crop. Explain how environmental stress can alter the balance.
questions.explanation: Crop growth is a balance between assimilate production and respiratory consumption.

questions.questionText: Outline a plant-breeding programme for improving drought tolerance in a maize population. Include selection, testing and release stages.
questions.explanation: Effective breeding combines a clearly defined target phenotype with repeated selection and multi-environment evaluation.

questions.questionText: Discuss integrated pest management (IPM) for a major field crop. Your answer should include monitoring, cultural, biological and chemical measures and explain why pesticide resistance should be managed.
questions.explanation: IPM combines compatible methods and reserves chemical control for economically justified situations.

questions.questionText: Explain the difference between genotype, phenotype and genotype × environment interaction, and discuss why G×E matters when selecting livestock.
questions.explanation: Selection decisions based on one environment may not predict performance elsewhere when G×E is substantial.

questions.questionText: A dairy ration supplies adequate crude protein but milk yield remains below target. Explain why crude-protein percentage alone may not guarantee adequate protein nutrition.
questions.explanation: Ration formulation must consider nutrient supply and utilisation, not crude protein alone.

questions.questionText: Explain how the rumen enables cattle to use fibrous feeds. Include microbial fermentation, volatile fatty acids and microbial protein.
questions.explanation: Symbiotic microbial fermentation allows ruminants to exploit cellulose-rich feeds.

questions.questionText: Design a grazing plan for a farm experiencing pasture degradation. Include stocking rate, rest periods, forage monitoring and actions during drought.
questions.explanation: Pasture sustainability requires matching animal demand with forage supply over time.

questions.questionText: A tractor engine is losing power and producing excessive smoke. Describe a systematic diagnostic procedure before major components are replaced.
questions.explanation: Systematic diagnosis avoids unnecessary replacement and identifies simple causes first.

questions.questionText: Explain price elasticity of demand and discuss two implications for a farmer selling a highly perishable crop.
questions.explanation: Elasticity is a percentage-based responsiveness concept; perishability affects marketing strategy and bargaining conditions.

questions.questionText: A farm has two enterprises. Enterprise A has a gross margin of $18,000 using 30 hectares; Enterprise B has a gross margin of $14,000 using 14 hectares. Calculate gross margin per hectare for each and interpret the result.
Discuss how soil organic matter influences soil structure, water relations, nutrient supply and biological activity.
questions.explanation: Organic matter is central to many physical, chemical and biological soil functions.

questions.questionText: Explain how rainfall intensity, soil cover, slope and infiltration interact to determine erosion risk on a cultivated field.
questions.explanation: Erosion results from interacting rainfall energy, soil susceptibility and runoff processes.

questions.questionText: A researcher compares three fertiliser treatments using four replicated plots per treatment. Explain why replication, randomisation and a control are important, and state what a statistically significant treatment effect would mean.
questions.explanation: Sound experimental design supports valid inference about treatment effects.

questions.questionText: Explain the significance of soil Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC) and Base Saturation Percentage in managing acidic red fersiallitic soils in Zimbabwe's Highveld, and show how calcitic vs dolomitic lime corrects acidity. [8 marks]
questions.explanation: High CEC buffers nutrients against leaching; acidic soils have high H⁺/Al³⁺ saturation causing phosphate fixation and Al toxicity to maize roots [3]. Calcitic lime (CaCO₃) neutralises H⁺ while supplying Ca²⁺; dolomitic lime (CaMg(CO₃)₂) supplies both Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ raising base saturation and pH into optimal 5.5–6.2 range [5].

questions.questionText: Draw/describe the typical classical Production Function (Stages I, II, and III) relating Total, Average, and Marginal Physical Product of nitrogen fertiliser applied to irrigated wheat, and explain why rational farmers operate ONLY in Stage II. [8 marks]
questions.explanation: Stage I: APP rises to peak (MPP > APP — still gaining increasing returns per kg N, so stopping early under-uses fixed land) [2.5]. Stage II: MPP > 0 but declining (APP > MPP > 0) — rational economic zone where optimal MVP = MFC profit point lies [3]. Stage III: MPP < 0 (toxic salt burn drops total yield, losing both money and grain) [2.5].

questions.questionText: Compare the roles of tissue culture micropropagation and marker-assisted selection (MAS) in accelerating Zimbabwean crop improvement (e.g., virus-free sweet potato/banana and drought-tolerant maize). [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Micropropagation cultures meristem tips on sterile nutrient-hormone media yielding thousands of uniform, virus-free clonal plantlets rapidly year-round [3]. MAS uses DNA markers linked to QTLs for drought/disease resistance to screen seedlings in the lab without waiting multiple field seasons [3].

questions.questionText: Evaluate the economic and ecological trade-offs of biological control, chemical pesticides, and Integrated Pest Management (IPM) against Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) in smallholder maize. [7 marks]
questions.explanation: Pure synthetic sprays act fast in acute outbreaks yet risk pesticide resistance, bee/predator mortality, and high cost [2.5]. Biological predators (parasitoid wasps/Bacillus thuringiensis) are eco-safe but slow under severe outbreaks [2]. IPM combines early scouting, push-pull intercropping (Desmodium), conserving natural enemies, and targeted low-toxicity spraying only above economic threshold [2.5].

questions.questionText: A commercial beef feedlot wants to formulate a 16% Crude Protein (CP) ration using Maize meal (9% CP) and Soya bean meal (44% CP). Using the Pearson Square method, calculate the percentage and kg of each ingredient in a 1,000 kg batch. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Center target = 16%. Maize difference: |44 - 16| = 28 parts. Soya difference: |9 - 16| = 7 parts. Total parts = 28 + 7 = 35 [3]. Maize = (28/35)×100% = 80% = 800 kg [1.5]. Soya meal = (7/35)×100% = 20% = 200 kg [1.5].

questions.questionText: Explain the physiological causes of heat stress in high-yielding Holstein dairy cows in Zimbabwe's Lowveld and propose four housing/nutritional engineering mitigations. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: High ambient temperature + humidity exceed evaporative panting/sweating capacity, raising respiration rate, lowering dry-matter feed intake, suppressing conception rates and milk yield [2]. Mitigations: high reflective insulated roofs with open ridge ventilation; sprinkler mist + fans in holding yards; abundant cool shaded water troughs; feeding energy-dense rations at cool night hours [4].

questions.questionText: Outline how partial budgeting differs from a whole-farm profit-and-loss budget, and list the four decision questions used in a Partial Budget when switching from manual weeding to boom-sprayer herbicides. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Whole-farm budgets cover every enterprise and fixed cost; partial budgeting evaluates ONLY marginal changes in costs and returns from a specific management tweak [2]. Four items: (1) Extra returns/yield saved + (2) Reduced costs (casual weeding wages saved) MINUS (3) Extra costs (herbicide, sprayer hire/fuel) + (4) Reduced revenue (if any). Positive net gain supports adopting herbicides [4].

questions.questionText: Describe the design components and hydraulic principles of a trickle/drip irrigation block, and explain why fertigation works best with drip systems. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Pump → sand/disc filter (essential to stop emitter clogging) → pressure regulator & non-return valve → fertigation injector → mainline/submain → lateral lines with pressure-compensating emitters at low operating pressure (1–2 bar) [3.5]. Fertigation injects soluble fertilisers directly into active wet root bulbs, minimising leaching/volatilisation and saving labour [2.5].

questions.questionText: Explain how mycorrhizal fungi and rhizobial bacteria form mutualistic symbioses with crop roots and describe two field practices that harm beneficial soil microbes. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Arbuscular mycorrhizal hyphae extend root surface area to absorb immobile phosphorus and water in return for plant sugars; Rhizobium fixes N₂ inside root nodules using host carbohydrates [4]. Harmed by: excessive continuous broad-spectrum soil fumigants/fungicides, severe waterlogging (killing aerobes), or burning all crop residues leaving bare hot soil [2].

questions.questionText: Assess three ways Zimbabwe's small-scale farmers can mitigate climate-induced rainfall variability through climate-smart agriculture (CSA). [6 marks]
questions.explanation: 1. Switching portions of hectarage to drought-tolerant small grains (sorghum, pearl millet, cowpeas) [2]. 2. Adopting Pfumvudza basins + tied ridges + mulching to harvest every drop of sporadic storms [2]. 3. Index-based weather micro-insurance and staggered planting dates guided by MSD seasonal forecasts [2].
